title: Berkshire 1996 letter: inevitables, float, incentives, and investing simply
summary: Buffett's 1996 letter reviews 36.1% net worth growth and explains intrinsic value, float cost, super-cat insurance discipline, and incentive pay. It also sets out his investing philosophy: own "Inevitables" with durable moats, stay inactive, avoid change, and admit mistakes like USAir.

principles.text: Buy an easily understandable business with earnings virtually certain to be higher in 5, 10, 20 years, at a rational price.
principles.quote: Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten and twenty years from now.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; knowing its boundary matters more than its size.
principles.quote: The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.

principles.text: Prefer certainty in stable, dominant businesses over hope in fast-changing industries.
principles.quote: Obviously many companies in high-tech businesses or embryonic industries will grow much faster in percentage terms than will The Inevitables. But I would rather be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable only if its cost is below the market cost of money; underwriting profit makes it free.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is an albatross if the cost of its float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones, and hold only shareholders who can tolerate volatility.
principles.quote: Charlie and I would much rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%.

principles.text: Design incentive pay to be tailored, simple, and tied to what participants control; shun lottery-ticket options.
principles.quote: Goals should be (1) tailored to the economics of the specific operating business; (2) simple in character so that the degree to which they are being realized can be easily measured; and (3) directly related to the daily activities of plan participants.
